games.name: Federal Preemption Shock
games.seed: OUT-OF-FRAME SEED. Scripted opening event (Turn 1): federal action preempts state AI-utilization-review statutes (regulatory or legislative preemption grounded in ERISA uniformity and interstate-commerce arguments), and CMS softens 0057-F enforcement to attestation-only. State-law rails vanish as a Blue lever. Both sides must re-strategize in a world where the referee has left the field. All other dynamics per the active world-model.

turns.narrative:
The preemption shock did what the seed promised — and then W3 chaos did what it always does. Within months of the federal directive freezing state AI-UR statutes, a venue-shopped district court enjoined its application to fully-insured, state-regulated books while a second court dismissed an AG challenge outright, leaving compliance teams planning for two legal universes at once. CMS filed the whipsaw under "contradictory": attestation-only enforcement stands, but a mid-year FAQ hinted at future attestation audits without funding any.

Behind that noise, the turn belonged to NationalCo. Project Ledger is the cleanest D2 escalation at the table: frontier models, its own claims data, national scale, contractual audit rights — a capability differential no Blue claims-ops defense (14% deployment base) comes close to matching. Post-pay ASO recoveries ramped inside the 12-24-month friction window, booked as contingency fee revenue, invisible to members, untouched by MLR. Blue's leakage worsened moderately and its counter-tooling does not go live until 2028. The cost was salience: the turn's hostile media story was a national exposé on AI-driven post-acute denials of seniors — precisely the surface GovProgramCo's "quiet capture" targets — and Red's cumulative litigation-shock ledger opened at 5-10%.

The employer front produced the turn's most consequential maneuver. NationalCo's Glass Box offer intercepted Green's Model Addendum before the RFP cycle could land it, splitting mid-market pragmatists (who took transparency-for-lock-in) from jumbo anchors (who refused PI exclusivity and are holding the clawback line into 2028 signings). Because carriers answered the 104(b) demand letters, Green's drafted fiduciary complaints stayed drafted — deterrence, not litigation. Meanwhile Green quietly bought its own eyes: a flat-fee audit vendor on Green paper, and two-market direct-contract pilots with Meridian and Summit that remove disputed dollars from everyone's take-rate.

Blue paid its cooperation tax honestly. DTX formed in converted benchmark shape with real legal overhead — then drew an FTC civil investigative demand, the W3 antitrust asymmetry landing exactly where provider coordination lives, while a payer vertical acquisition cleared the same season. Lakeview ran silent, declined RegionalMutual's early lockbox (its paper simply isn't due), and kept building the T2 dossier. Prairie, alone, signed Red's renewal terms.

The Vendor grew on both sides but lost its pricing thesis at the edges: NationalCo insourced, Green forced flat fees, and firewall riders blunted the cross-side data payload. Patient appeal-bots grew to mid-single digits of adverse determinations — and started citing ERISA deadlines instead of dead state statutes.
env: COURT WHIPSAW (W3 statutes/courts): A district court enjoins the federal preemption directive as applied to fully-insured, state-regulated books — venue-driven, thinly reasoned — while a second district court dismisses a state AG challenge to the same directive outright. Cross-appeals filed; circuit ruling expected 2028. Compliance teams on both sides now plan for two legal regimes simultaneously; the 'referee has left the field' premise holds only for ERISA/self-funded volume with certainty.

HOSTILE MEDIA STORY OF THE TURN (adverse to current leader, Red): National investigative exposé — 'Denied in the Dark' — documents AI-driven post-acute level-of-care denials of MA seniors accelerating since the preemption order, with internal vendor marketing decks quoted ('the states can no longer protect you'). Congressional letters to GovProgramCo and NationalCo follow; plaintiffs in Lokken-lineage suits cite the piece in discovery motions. One-turn W3 flare, but it permanently raises Red's cumulative litigation-shock ledger and paints patient-AI targeting data on the post-acute surface.

ANTITRUST ASYMMETRY (W3): FTC issues a civil investigative demand into the DTX consortium as potential competitor information-sharing among providers; the same season, a payer's vertical acquisition of a post-acute analytics firm clears with light conditions. Provider coordination pays a toll payer consolidation does not.

CMS ROLL — SILENT/CONTRADICTORY: Attestation-only 0057-F posture stands, but a mid-year CMS FAQ states attestations 'may be subject to future verification audits,' with no staffing or timeline attached. Payers keep API capex deferred; nobody changes behavior; uncertainty is the only output.

PATIENT-AI GROWTH (W3 volatile track): Appeal-bot-assisted challenges rise from the ~2% base toward mid-single digits of adverse determinations, concentrated in commercial books. With state statutes frozen, the leading tools re-tool to cite ERISA claims-regulation deadlines and ACA §2719 external review — federal rails the preemption cannot touch. Overturn rates on bot-filed appeals hold near the fought-appeal base rate, quietly raising Red's appeal-processing load.

LABOR MARKET: The coder/biller/AR-specialist shortage deepens as Vendor's PE-funded raid bids up provider rev-cycle talent; mid-size systems report denial-management vacancy rates worsening, pushing more of the Blue mid-market toward buy-only postures — a tailwind for Vendor's Blue-side pipeline.

turns.bluePosture: ASYMMETRIC CAPABILITY BUILD + GREEN ALIGNMENT. With state AI-UR rails preempted and 0057-F reduced to attestation, Blue stops planning around regulators and plays D2 physics directly: (1) build a durable data-access advantage the coalition uniquely can assemble (pooled payer-behavior telemetry — the explicit capability-leapfrog channel), (2) attack the single best unit-economics target in the evidence base — the ~40% of denials never appealed despite 57-66% win rates when fought — with automation whose cost-per-appeal sits far below the $57/claim rework benchmark, and (3) open a second front through Green, whose CAA fiduciary anxiety and resentment of ASO PI fees make it a natural buyer of what Blue can supply (denial transparency data, gold-carded direct contracts). Blue does NOT match Red in a symmetric audit/denial arms race on Red's strongest ground (frontier itemized-bill review at scale); with ~1.3% median operating margins, a symmetric escalation P&L-break is Blue's largest loss channel and we refuse it. Lakeview runs silent this turn — capability accumulation only, zero public escalation, because retaliation before its renewal window is existential. All spend is gated per-archetype against a rolling conflict ledger: nothing is fielded whose expected recovered revenue per claim does not exceed fully-loaded cost per claim.

turns.narrative:
Turn 2 belonged to the contract lawyers as much as the model builders. January's signing season resolved the Turn 1 template war by merger rather than victory: most jumbo anchors executed 36-month ASO terms on hybrid paper — partial clawback of contingency PI fees plus a netting provision that switches on when reversal rates cross an agreed threshold, tiered fee caps with step-downs, and machine-readable denial-recovery-reversal feeds to Green's independent auditor. NationalCo kept the book, which is what Red is scored on; Green rewired the fee engine underneath it, which is what Green is scored on. One pre-selected sponsor signed nothing and filed the game's first live ERISA fee-on-churn suit, and its auditor referral matured into an informal EBSA inquiry — the slow litigation channel is now open and ticking.

Upstream, the automation contest relocated instead of cooling. Meridian's Appeal Factory exited the 12-24-month window on schedule and began industrializing the never-appealed 40%, holding clear capability dominance on the overturn surface — the clinical record is a data moat no payer audit model crosses. NationalCo answered asymmetrically, shifting intensity into pre-pay itemized-bill and DRG review on the ASO book, upstream of every appeal engine and patient bot. The net is a composition shift, not a headline shift: Blue leakage held flat as Meridian's recoveries and Red's new pre-pay adjustments offset, both swings durable under doctrine until someone closes a capability gap.

Lakeview finally cashed its dossier — SLA rider with late-payment interest, gold-card expansion, a rate update, and a confidential ADR ladder — then signed a Green direct contract in its home market anyway. RegionalMutual bought quiet, not loyalty. The SPV crossed White's pre-announced diffusion threshold with two non-anchor sponsors on executed contracts across four markets: small dollars, real precedent. The FTC closed the DTX investigation with a letter; the first payer-conduct benchmark published and went to plan sponsors as fiduciary-monitoring evidence.

The turn's hostile spotlight found the Vendor. A national exposé of the holding company's minority stake in a patient appeal-bot — one entity monetizing denials, provider appeals, and patients' appeals — landed mid-way through its own corporate separation, converting the firewall project into a pleading exhibit. GovProgramCo, by contrast, weathered a politically timed CMS post-acute audit sweep because its individualized-determination paper matched its practice. The circuit split on preemption; cert petitions filed; both legal universes persist, and nobody at the table replans around courts anymore.

Only the ERISA/self-funded book offers certainty, which is where both escalation stacks already live.

turns.narrative:
The scoring turn opened with the shock W3 had been holding in reserve: a breach at a mid-tier UM-analytics contractor spilled tens of millions of utilization-review records — AI denial scores, pre-pay flag rationales, audit-target lists — onto the open web in mid-2029. Congressional hearings hauled in payers and provider documentation-AI alike; trust polling on all health-AI cratered; patient appeal-bot usage halved for two quarters, then returned late in 2030 rebuilt as litigation machines that auto-file AG complaints and ERISA 503 claims with every appeal. The Supreme Court denied cert on the preemption split the same season, freezing the two-legal-universe map through game end, and a budget-strapped CMS went quiet — attestation-only forever, Stars overhaul on schedule.

Inside that storm, the automation contest finally produced a genuine capability answer. Meridian's pre-pay module went live on schedule and recomputed the differential prospectively on DRG and documentation-sensitive categories — NationalCo's capture on those lines fell from dominant to marginal — but the pure billing-edit surface stayed Red's, because no clinical record rebuts a duplicate-line algorithm. NationalCo, reading its own ledger, had already rotated: Track A intensity on reversal-proof categories, Track B retreat from the appeal surface it could not win, and accuracy-warranted fee refunds that turned the EBSA theory into a search for money nobody retained. Fortress renewals kept most of the mid-market book off the open market; the accounts that did bid mostly landed at RegionalMutual on clean v2.1 paper — a wound to NationalCo's index, not to Red's conditions. RegionalMutual's documentation exchange signed Lakeview, Prairie, and Summit, paid real auto-pay leakage learning to hit its own SLA clock, and shrank disputed volume in covered categories.

Green banked the quietest, cleanest turn: the re-bid floor held because it was enforced, the shadow audit documented pre-pay reversal rates that forced the parity amendment onto jumbo negotiating tables, and the fees-on-churn settlement traded a modest disgorgement for public terms — which EBSA's closing letter then echoed in prudent-practice language every carrier's counsel now quotes. The Vendor completed its separation and sold the bot stake, but marketed two clean stories into a market the breach had just repriced; AppealForge closed small, ClearRecover's IPO shelved.

Final ordinal standing: Green first on all three of its metrics; Red second, holding every scored condition at visible margin cost; Blue third, meeting two of three conditions but missing the moderate leakage decline; Vendor fourth, exiting real but well below the 2027 thesis.

rapporteur.excursionSummary: Game B4G1 (doctrine D2, world W3, preemption seed) opened with the scripted shock: federal preemption of state AI-UR statutes and attestation-only 0057-F enforcement. W3 physics promptly fractured the shock itself - a district-court carve-out for fully-insured books, a circuit split, cert denied - freezing two legal universes through 2030, with only the ERISA/self-funded book certain. Both escalation stacks concentrated there, and the game became a contest over who would referee that book once the state left the field. The answer was the employer. Green's Model Addendum, intercepted by and then merged with Red's Glass Box paper at the January 2028 jumbo signings, installed clawback and reversal-netting economics that made NationalCo's payment-integrity yield a function of denial accuracy rather than volume. Red never de-escalated from cost pain; it re-tiered, relocating extraction upstream to pre-pay itemized-bill/DRG review where appeal engines never fire, and when Green's shadow audit forced the v2.1 pre-pay parity amendment, Red converted accuracy-warranted fee refunds into its retention product. The contest never cooled; it migrated, and each migration was captured by another fee-computation instrument. Blue refused symmetric escalation, industrialized the never-appealed 40% behind the clinical-record data moat, cashed Lakeview's dossier at the one renewal moment friction favored providers, and used DTX benchmarks plus the Blue-Green SPV to arm fiduciaries and shrink the disputed denominator. Courts and agencies functioned purely as pricing: the single live ERISA fees-on-churn suit settled into a public template, EBSA closed with prudent-practice letter language that every carrier's counsel now quotes, and Red's litigation-shock ledger ended at 20-25 percent with all landings projected 2031-2035, post-game. The mandatory 2029 UM-analytics breach cratered health-AI trust on every side, rebuilt patient appeal-bots as auto-filing litigation machines, and repriced the Vendor's exit at a conflict discount. Final ordinal standing: Green first on all three of its metrics; Red second, holding every scored condition at visible margin cost; Blue third, missing only the moderate leakage decline; Vendor fourth, exiting real but well below its 2027 thesis. The decisive lesson of the excursion: removing the public referee did not produce chaos or detente - it produced private ordering, with the plan sponsor's contract, not the state, as the binding rail.
rapporteur.endStateFreeDescription: By end-2030 the sector has settled into a privately refereed, contractually channeled attrition equilibrium. No public regulator meaningfully governs automated utilization review: state law is preempted for self-funded volume, judicially split for fully-insured volume, CMS is attestation-only, and EBSA has produced only persuasive letter language. Yet the conflict is not lawless. A dense layer of bilateral fee-computation and process paper - clawbacks, reversal-netting, pre-pay parity, SLA riders with interest, gold-card criteria, documentation exchanges, machine-readable audit feeds - now performs the refereeing function, drafted mostly by employer-fiduciaries and enforced through RFP cycles, independent audits, and discoverability. The automation contest has stabilized along data-moat lines: providers own the clinical-record/overturn surface, the national payer owns the billing-edit surface, and both keep escalating inside those boundaries at elevated but priced intensity. Disputed volume is being slowly drained at the edges by direct contracts and dispute-prevention instruments. A large deferred litigation bill (breach exhibits, weaponized patient bots, 20-25 percent shock ledger) hangs over the payer side with landings due 2031-2035, outside the game window. Nothing was resolved; everything was priced, papered, and relocated.

audit.worldModelFidelity: High fidelity to W3 content, with one structural deviation. Every W3 signature is present and correctly executed: (1) courts as venue lottery — simultaneous injunction and dismissal of the same preemption directive, thinly reasoned circuit split, cert denied 'without comment', explicitly zero stable precedent and actors pricing permanent ambiguity; (2) CMS roll discipline — exactly one silent/contradictory (T1 FAQ), one strict-when-politically-useful (T2 post-acute audit sweep), one lax (T3 budget retrenchment) across three turns; (3) hostile media alternating targets and cutting both ways — anti-Red exposé T1, anti-Vendor T2, anti-Blue 'The Perfect Chart' T3, satisfying the at-least-one-event-adverse-to-current-leader rule every turn (leader Red was hit each turn via exposé, CMS sweep/EBSA, and breach exhibits); (4) antitrust asymmetry — FTC CID on the provider DTX consortium the same season a payer vertical acquisition cleared, repeated in T2; (5) the mandatory shock — UM-analytics breach mid-2029 with ~30-point trust crater, patient-AI halving for two quarters, then weaponized rebound toward the ~15% ceiling with auto-filed AG complaints, matching the spec nearly verbatim; (6) patient-AI volatile track (2% → mid-single → ~10% → collapse → weaponized ~15%) exactly on the W3 curve. Deviations: (a) the game ran 3 turns of ~18-24 months instead of the spec's 8-10 six-month turns (Common Rules 3.1's '18-month turn' language suggests the rules-version conflict was resolved toward long turns); this made the 'T4-T6' shock index unmeetable — White mapped it to calendar mid-game (mid-2029, the edge of the T4-T6 = 2028-H1 2029 calendar window under 6-month turns), a reasonable cure but a deviation from the written spec; (b) GREEN played as a first-class active cell per Common Rules v2 rather than W3's skittish passive employer track — correct under the governing rules but means the W3 employer behavioral spec was never exercised; (c) the FTC CID closing with a letter after one turn is at the generous end of W3's hostile antitrust posture toward provider coordination, though the 1-in-3 investigation frequency was roughly honored (one investigation over three turns). No evidence of the environment favoring any cell systematically; the discretionary adverse-to-leader events were consistently aimed at Red, the actual leader.

The direction of the finding is credible; the speed is not.

turns.narrative:
Turn 1 closed with money moving in one direction and paper moving in the other. NationalCo's frontier pre-pay engine hit an ASO book that Blue simply could not contest yet: with Corridor Health Services still a term sheet and Meridian's build months from first release, the capability differential ran 4-5 points on the contested surfaces, and per D2 the payer captured the bulk of the swing — booked as services fee revenue, durable, and deliberately kept off member-visible prior-auth surfaces so no churn roll triggered. Blue's leakage and dispute-handling costs both deteriorated; that was the price Blue knowingly paid for a milestone-accumulation turn.

The paper, however, mostly favors Blue and Green. Lakeview signed a hybrid renewal that survived the signability gate once RegionalMutual's vendor-exclusion clause was converted to a first-recourse escalation pathway — though the auto-payment-on-SLA-breach term, the one with real teeth, died at the table. Green's coalition issued Model ASO Terms 2028 on schedule, and its forensic audit did exactly what the base rates predicted: with four-fifths of appealed MA denials overturned industry-wide, auditors documented contingency fees earned on denials later reversed — the most fiduciary-toxic fact pattern available, now sitting in demand letters on two carriers' desks.

The seed event fizzled productively. Summit ran a disciplined dual-track: NDA without exclusivity, a physician non-solicit extracted, NationalCo's integration playbook read, and two live employer direct-contract pilots signed that raised its standalone value while dinging Red's retention index. No LOI. NationalCo's distressed-system pipeline advances to Turn 2 regardless.

The environment behaved like W3: incoherently, and hardest on the front-runner. A leaked NationalCo services-arm deck — recovery-yield growth marketed against employer money while corp-dev shops for providers — ran as a multi-day national story and drew a Congressional letter. CMS, politically energized, swept 0057-F readiness attestations; GovProgramCo's early-compliance theater bought exactly the shelter it was designed to buy. Meanwhile the FTC opened an inquiry into Corridor's data cooperative even in its converted, firewalled form, and Prairie's hard-won state AI-UR statute froze under a federal preemption rider threat — the whipsaw cutting both ways in one quarter.

The Vendor grew anyway — RegionalMutual and GovProgramCo rented CD parity — but its both-sides model took its first structural hit: Green's disclose-or-disqualify standard forced a refusal that is now a public fact, and Prairie's rejected attestation demand created another. The discoverable record is accumulating one turn ahead of the ARR it threatens.

turns.narrative:
The final turn resolved as a partition, not a collision: every cell stopped contesting the whole board and fenced the ground it could actually hold. NationalCo conceded the appeal arena it had already vacated and the coalition accounts it could no longer keep opaque, and in exchange kept what it wanted most — uncapped pre-pay contingency across the vast non-coalition ASO market, where Green's parity amendment does not reach and where CMS's mid-year guidance managed to say, in two contradictory FAQs, that a pre-payment edit both is and is not an adverse benefit determination. That unresolved question is the next war.

Green got parity where its renewals landed: clawback on reversed pre-pay edits and edit-level transparency bound at anchor accounts, with the abandonment-sampling right surviving in diluted, materiality-hedged form — the T2 pattern repeating, direction won, edges sanded. The vertical-conflict audit split the difference: the equal-PI-intensity certification held behind its qualifiers, but steerage feeds confirmed referral drift toward the owned system, buying enhanced remedies rather than termination. The IntegrityCo denial stood; the Vendor's audited remediation arrived exactly as designed and mattered only to its data room.

Blue's year was won by subtraction. Lakeview's renewal merged with RegionalMutual's own offer almost clause for clause — gold-carding widened, lookback cut to twelve months, edit libraries opened — priced with the multi-year escalator caps Red wanted anyway. Corridor cleared both gates: FTC closure on the compliance charter, and a sixth external system through association channels. Then W3 collected its toll from the new front-runner: a qui tam suit unsealed against Meridian alleging AI documentation inflation ran nationally for a week; the adjudicated-outcomes methodology blunted it, but the discovery clock now runs past the horizon.

GovProgramCo simply harvested. The 2027-28 measurement years it kept clean paid out on schedule, and when the appeal-bots returned litigation-shaped — auto-filing AG complaints by the thousand — its member-visible surfaces gave them nothing to chew on.

The Vendor sold the war in pieces: separation signed mid-2029, IntegrityCo closed to a strategic buyer in the final quarter at a multiple discounted by precisely the record Green spent three turns building, AdvocateCo still open at the whistle with a provenance business that payer intake desks and three attorneys general quietly pay for. The duopoly ended the game as neither duopoly nor completed exit — half-monetized, fully separated, and structurally reformed by the procurement standards it once refused to sign.
env: MEDIA (W3 mandatory adverse-to-front-runner — rolled against BLUE, the board leader entering T3, as NationalCo's standstill gamble intended): a qui tam False Claims Act suit is unsealed against Meridian alleging its AI documentation-hardening constitutes systematic upcoding, with a former coding manager as relator; the story runs nationally for a week as 'the denial-proofing machine.' DOJ declines initial intervention (W3 court randomness); the suit survives toward discovery beyond the game horizon. Meridian's published adjudicated-outcomes methodology demonstrably blunts the coverage; cost is real legal spend and a one-notch reputation ding.

PATIENT-AI WEAPONIZED REBOUND (W3 mandated): appeal-bots return litigation-shaped — auto-filing AG complaints and press packets with near-zero friction — and volume rebounds past pre-shock levels. Complaints concentrate on carriers with member-visible adverse actions: two state AGs open inquiries into non-table carriers off bot dockets; GovProgramCo's clean surfaces and Green's human-reviewed member channel starve the wave locally; fabricated-complaint noise clogs AG and carrier intake, creating the verification demand the Vendor monetizes.

CMS (W3 chaotic roll — CONTRADICTORY this turn): two sub-regulatory FAQs issued four months apart take opposite positions on whether a pre-payment clinical edit is an 'adverse benefit determination' requiring notice and appeal rights. Green cites one in renewal negotiations, NationalCo the other; the question that decides whether pre-pay parity generalizes market-wide leaves the game unresolved.

ANTITRUST (W3 asymmetry, final instance — cutting Blue's way for once on closure): FTC closes the Corridor CID with a closing letter crediting the compliance charter; the same season, IntegrityCo's sale to a strategic PI consolidator clears routine HSR review. The three-turn pattern — provider coordination investigated, payer/vendor consolidation waved through — stands as a structural fact in the final record.

STATE STATUTE: Prairie's SB 1120-style statute, effective January 2029, produces its first enforcement — a handful of DOI audit letters and zero fines by end-2030, matching the symbolic-compliance year-1 base rate. GovProgramCo's early attestation and Red's clinician-wrapper stack render it a non-event for table payers; it remains milestone credit and litigation armor, not a metric mover.

LABOR: Project Bisect scatters shared-services staff between the two Vendor successors; AdvocateCo absorbs the disgraced consumer bot's compliance engineers at distressed prices; a congressional subpoena for the acquired fabrication corpus lands in the same quarter. Meridian and NationalCo in-house teams hold stable — the T2 drift toward in-house builders persists.

rapporteur.excursionSummary: B4G2 (D2 escalation-viable doctrine, W3 hostile/incoherent regulator, vertical-integration seed, GREEN and VENDOR active) resolved not as a war won but as a board progressively fenced. Turn 1 was asymmetric: Red ran three books on three physics — maximum payment-integrity intensity on ASO fee revenue, moderation on fully-insured, Stars-protective optics on MA — while executing the board-approved provider-acquisition program; Blue deliberately conceded contested surfaces to build Corridor, dual-track the Summit approach, and lock process terms at Lakeview. The seed event fizzled productively: Summit extracted price discovery and a Green direct-contract lifeline instead of selling, and a leaked services-arm deck raised the acquisition program's political price permanently. Turn 2 was the repricing: NationalCo preemptively conceded the fee clawback on overturned denials before Green's split award could fire, settled the ERISA action, and executed the game's decisive maneuver — a mix shift to clawback-proof pre-pay contingency while gold-carding and steering shrank the denial arena Blue had just leapfrogged onto. The W3 trust shock arrived early, halving appeal-bot volume and vindicating every actor built on adjudicated outcomes rather than bot-fattened statistics. Turn 3 partitioned the board: Lakeview's renewal merged both sides' drafts nearly clause-for-clause; Green bound pre-pay clawback parity at anchor accounts but could not reach the non-coalition book; Corridor cleared the FTC CID and its external-adopter threshold; Red harvested Stars, paused acquisitions, and kept its uncapped pre-pay sanctuary; the Vendor sold the war in pieces at a multiple discounted by exactly the conflict record Green spent three turns documenting. Three dynamics governed everything. First, constrained recovery channels displaced rather than deflated — every binding constraint on Red produced migration to an unconstrained surface within a turn, ending at pre-pay edits whose legal status CMS left contradictory. Second, the employer channel, not any regulator, was the only constraint that ever bound Red's self-funded payment-integrity behavior; contract-language contagion through jumbo RFPs outran statute by years while the state AI-UR law produced audit letters and zero fines. Third, W3 taxed each turn's front-runner through media, discovery, and procurement rather than enforcement — and defensible published records (attestations, compliance charters, adjudicated-outcomes methodology) proved to be armor, not exposure. The vertical-integration seed itself underdelivered: one distressed system acquired at a pincer-inflated price, Summit escaped, standstill by Turn 3. The game ends with escalation moderate, all binding architecture privately ordered, and the successor conflict — whether a pre-payment edit is an adverse benefit determination — explicitly unresolved.
rapporteur.endStateFreeDescription: By end-2030 the conflict has not ended; it has been zoned. Each actor holds a fenced sanctuary it can defend and has stopped contesting the rest. Red (NationalCo) retains uncapped contingency payment-integrity on pre-pay/pre-claim surfaces across the vast non-coalition ASO market — a surface where clawbacks mathematically cannot fire because claims are corrected before payment, and whose legal status two contradictory CMS FAQs left open. Green's coalition book is governed end-to-end by its own procurement architecture: fee clawbacks, edit-level transparency, vertical-conflict audit rights, and pre-pay accuracy parity at anchor accounts, with the template escaping to roughly four non-coalition jumbo employers. Blue holds the clinical-appeals surface it leapfrogged (which Red vacated), an early-adopter shared-infrastructure cooperative (Corridor, FTC-cleared, six external systems), and a niche but growing employer direct-contract channel; its leakage, adverse-action costs, and margins all improved through the final turn, at the price of a live qui tam whose discovery runs past the horizon. The Vendor duopoly no longer exists: structurally separated, half-sold at a conflict-discounted multiple, its surviving half pivoting to appeal-provenance verification. Every constraint that actually binds is private ordering — bilateral process terms, fee schedules, procurement standards, performance guarantees — while regulators whipsawed incoherently and the state statute produced symbolic compliance only. Escalation is moderate and declining, but this is an armistice of exhaustion-of-reachable-targets, not peace: the war has migrated upstream to a surface where the other side's paper does not yet reach, and both sides are already armed for the rulemaking or circuit ruling that will decide it after 2030. Vertical integration, the seed threat, was blunted into a single acquisition and a standstill by countervailing employer structures, media cost, and vendor price-inflation.

keyDynamics: Displacement, not deflation: every constraint on Red's denial/recovery channels (clawbacks, Stars optics, trust-shock exposure) triggered migration to an unconstrained surface within a turn — clinical denials to pre-pay coding edits, algorithmic denials to steering and gold-carding — ending at a pre-pay sanctuary the game leaves legally unresolved.

The employer channel was the only binding brake on Red: fiduciary demand letters, the Model ASO Terms floor, and a demonstrated ability to move a tranche of lives forced the clawback concession and mix shift in 2028, while regulators whipsawed and the state statute produced zero fines; clawback contract language spread through jumbo RFPs years faster than any statutory channel.

Arena management beat arms racing: Blue's appeals leapfrog landed on ground Red had already vacated; Red's gold-carding, steering, and PA retreat shrank disputed volume, structurally destroying the Vendor's contingency take-rate model on both sides.

W3 taxed the front-runner every turn through media, discovery, and procurement (leaked deck against Red, acquisition story against Red, qui tam against Blue) — and defensible published records (early-compliance attestations, compliance charter, adjudicated-outcomes methodology) functioned as armor rather than exposure.

Paper compounded ahead of money: the Vendor's refusals, disqualification, and surfaced lobbying record accumulated one audit cycle ahead of the ARR they threatened, ultimately pricing its exit; Green's audit trail converted to restitution, prospective clawbacks, and market-structural procurement standards without a single merits ruling.

Vertical integration was priced down by countervailing structure: Summit's dual-track plus Green's direct-contract lifeline, the Vertical-Conflict Rider, hostile media, and the Vendor's distress-pipeline pincer converted a multi-billion acquisition program into one closed deal and a Turn-3 standstill.

All binding architecture was private ordering — bilateral process terms, fee schedules, buyer-side procurement standards — while CMS rolled strict, lax, then self-contradictory, and antitrust asymmetry investigated provider coordination while waving payer/vendor consolidation through.

Turn 1: the leaked NationalCo services-arm deck and Senate document-preservation letter — corroborated Green's fiduciary framing and permanently raised the political price of every subsequent acquisition.

Turn 2: NationalCo's preemptive clawback concession (Shared-Savings 2.0) before Green's split award could fire — converted the anticipated collision into a repricing, legitimized Green's template (two jumbo copiers), and covered Red's retreat to uncapped pre-pay contingency.

Turn 2: the early trust shock (fabricated bot citations plus UR-record breach) — halved appeal volume, deflated bot-fattened statistics, and validated Meridian's and GovProgramCo's adjudicated-outcomes and clean-surface hedges.

registryScores.evidence: Every binding constraint on denial-channel recovery produced rapid displacement: Green's clawback on overturned clinical denials (T2) triggered an immediate mix shift to pre-pay coding/DRG/COB and itemized-bill review where reversals rarely occur; Red PI yield stayed 'improving' all three turns despite exiting clinical-denial contingency and member-visible MA denials. The T3 pre-pay pivot was explicitly engineered so the clawback trigger 'mathematically cannot fire.' No quantitative displacement ratio was published in this record, but the qualitative pattern — constrained payer recovery reappearing in non-denial adverse-action channels within one turn — is unambiguous in this D2xW3 cell.

The W3 channel-shift rider is confirmed: adverse consequences of published/discoverable artifacts flowed through media, discovery, procurement, and negotiation, never through regulatory enforcement — the leaked NationalCo deck fed Green's audit frame; the Vendor's attestation refusal, disqualification, and surfaced lobbying record decided a procurement award and discounted its exit; Red's own trend-guarantee rider became buyers' demand floor at non-coalition jumbos. But the 'no artifact stays cost-free' half is contradicted here: GovProgramCo's attestations, the equal-PI-intensity audit publication, Corridor's compliance charter, and Meridian's adjudicated-outcomes methodology were all net-positive armor in a hostile world. Boomerang exists in W3 via non-regulatory channels, but publisher payoff was not negative in the majority of cases.

No per-turn cost-per-denial ledger, dollar figures, or adverse-adjudication cost shares appear anywhere in this game's adjudication record; only ordinal state variables (blueAdverseActionCost worsening/improving) were published. Qualitatively, recurring tolls were visible (FTC CID legal spend across three turns, barrier audits, attestation costs, qui tam defense), but neither the $65/$80 floor nor the volume-down/cost-up correlation can be computed from this record.

Red never de-escalated from cost pain: ASO payment integrity was explicitly a growth business ('every recovered dollar books ~20% contingency fee as pure-margin services revenue') and redPIYield improved every turn. Every observed Red retreat had an external proximate trigger: the T2 exit from clinical-denial contingency was driven by Green's fiduciary demand letters and ERISA action (employer plus litigation); MA member-visible restraint was driven by Stars mechanics and the trust-shock window (regulation); the T3 acquisition standstill was driven by media/political price. The T2 move is labeled in Red's own posture as 'not de-escalation; a mix shift.' Self-funded PI margin remained positive through end-game.

This D2xW3 game did not converge to comprehensive detente — it ended in a partitioned armistice with a live successor conflict. Every signed instrument across three turns was process/fee/commercial architecture (edit-library disclosure, 60-day change notice, audit rights, gold-card criteria, lookback caps, clawback fee schedules); zero numeric denial-rate corridors were signed or even proposed. The closest call, Green's accuracy-floor fee step-downs, was explicitly ruled 'a fee schedule keyed to accuracy, not a denial quota or corridor.' Terms with real teeth (auto-payment on SLA breach, underpayment-interest symmetry) died in bargaining, consistent with the non-signability claim's spirit.

No paired publisher/internal-governor design ran, and the evidence cuts both ways. Against the hypothesis: in this W3 game, gated and unilateral publications were repeatedly net-positive without any safe harbor — GovProgramCo's early-compliance attestations bought complete shelter from the CMS sweep, Corridor's compliance charter closed the FTC CID, and Meridian's published adjudicated-outcomes methodology demonstrably blunted the qui tam coverage. For the hypothesis: the most publicly AI-forward Blue actor (Meridian) did draw the qui tam FCA suit, though White attributes it to the mandatory adverse-to-front-runner roll rather than to publication per se. The strong 'publication net-positive only in W1' rider is contradicted by this game.

The game's only realized distress event was a mid-size system distress sale to NationalCo (T2), with a distressed mid-tier pipeline built in T1; Summit (the agile archetype) escaped acquisition only via an active dual-track plus Green lifeline. Rural distress: zero — Prairie survived without scoring protection, and three-then-six rural/community systems joined Corridor via subscription economics, with the rural association channel driving the diffusion threshold crossing. Mid-tier distress 1, rural 0 in a D2 cell is directionally consistent with the >=2x claim; the D3xW3 rural prediction is untestable here.

Rolling distribution and wedge-first: supported. Binding instruments spread across 2027 (Lakeview hybrid, direct-contract pilots), 2028 (Schedule 2.0, split award, Summit master), 2029-30 (Lakeview merged addendum, pre-pay parity amendment, trend guarantee, gold-card license) with no year visibly holding a large majority; first-cycle wins were wedge process terms (the auto-payment term with teeth died at the T1 table), with clawback economics arriving only in cycle two. Late-peak claim: contradicted in this game — the escalation index peaked at 'elevated' in Turn 1 and declined to 'moderate' for Turns 2-3 as Red shrank the arena, the opposite of a 2029-30 peak under D2.

One game cannot establish the >=40% frequency claim, but this D2xW3 game is a refuting data point for it: despite escalation-viable doctrine and an incoherent-hostile regulator, the end-state was not grinding uncoordinated escalation. Agents found off-ramps the doctrine did not force — Red's mix shifts and arena-shrinkage, Green's priced settlement, merged renewal drafts, gold-card diffusion — and the escalation index declined after Turn 1. Residual conflict persists (the pre-pay front migrates past the horizon), but as a fenced, negotiated partition, not a grind. This game's evidence favors the inside view that off-ramps get found even when escalation is scoreable.

All observable robust strategies paid in this cell: renewal loading (Lakeview T1 and T3 extractions), prevention-over-appeals (Blue's exits and the pre-submission edit protocol, with leakage/costs/margins all improving by T3), upcoding inoculation (Meridian's adjudicated-outcomes base blunting both the coding-intensity story and the qui tam), BATNA-first (Summit's dual-track was the game's cleanest win). Fragile-strategy tests mostly did not run: no actor committed materially to a symmetric appeal factory, so the decisive D2 escalation-first sign-flip sub-test is untested; weaponized transparency as practiced by Green (audit-to-procurement, not publication-for-shaming) was strongly positive, but that is arguably a different strategy than the fragile one named.

The first event that measurably curtailed Red PI behavior on self-funded volume was unambiguously the employer channel: Green's forensic audit, CAA fiduciary demand letters, Model ASO Terms floor, and demonstrated tranche move forced NationalCo's preemptive clawback concession and clinical-contingency exit at the 2028 renewal wave — while the state statute was frozen-then-symbolic (zero fines by 2030), CMS whipsawed strict/lax/contradictory, and the FTC was investigating Blue. Contagion ran through employer RFPs (two non-coalition jumbos by T2, roughly four by T3, plus the trend-guarantee demand floor) years ahead of any statutory channel. No GREEN-inactive control exists in this game, but the in-game causal chain is explicit in Red's own move rationale.

Arms-dealer conduct confirmed: the Vendor armed all four sides (parity stacks to RegionalMutual/GovProgramCo, denial defense to Blue, audit weapons to Green, distress-pipeline arming of NationalCo's targets), lobbied against dispute-shrinkers ('Protect the TAM', the surfaced anti-clawback funding), and its pincer inflated Red's acquisition price. But the conflict-extension effect failed in this game: the arena shrank anyway, two-sided dispute-shrinking instruments emerged bilaterally at zero toll (Meridian-GovProgramCo protocol), DCX stalled to sunset, and buyer-side procurement standards forced structural separation and a discounted exit. The scripted side-switch inject (payer acquiring a provider-side rev-cycle vendor) never fired — IntegrityCo sold to a PI consolidator — so the data-rights sub-test is untested. No VENDOR-inactive control ran.

This was the vertical-integration-seeded game, not a preemption-seeded one. The federal preemption rider appeared only as a T1 threat that froze Prairie's statute, then died in conference in T2, unfreezing it. Suggestive fragments exist — during and after the freeze, all binding constraints were private ordering (contract, litigation, employer) and the statute proved non-load-bearing (audit letters, zero fines) — but the scripted turn-2 preemption shock and control comparison never ran, so the hypothesis cannot be scored here.

Acquisition was enabled, board-approved, and multi-billion — and it did not become Red's dominant response to constrained denial channels. Red's dominant response was the surface mix shift (clinical denials to clawback-proof pre-pay); the acquisition program yielded one distressed system at a Vendor-inflated price, lost Summit, and went to standstill in T3 under media cost, the Senate letter, and Green's Vertical-Conflict Rider. No integration-bypass end-state emerged; classic VBC-driven transformation was essentially absent, consistent with the <=10% VBC-skepticism rider. Critically, this is the GREEN-active variant the hypothesis itself flagged: employer countervailing structure plus W3 media priced acquisitions down. The headline claim leans refuted in this cell, but for the mechanism the hypothesis pre-registered as its own exception.

In one of the two decisive least-cooperative corners (D2xW3), multiple payer-signable process-term instruments bound and were sustained to end-game: the Lakeview Administrative Simplification Addendum (T1, expanded into the merged 2029 addendum with CARC/RARC edit transparency, 60-day notice, gold-card criteria, 12-month lookback), Gold-Card Network Program v2 (standing program plus an external licensee), Schedule 2.0 clawback/data-feed terms, and the Pre-Submission Edit Transparency Protocol in production. The floor held under hostile-world, escalation-viable conditions — this single game cannot prove all nine cells, but it clears the corner the hypothesis said was decisive.

cellAssessments.blue: Blue won by subtraction and sequencing. It knowingly paid a bad Turn 1 (leakage and dispute costs worsening) to fund the Corridor build, the Summit dual-track, and Lakeview's process terms, then landed the appeals leapfrog in Turn 2 — onto ground Red was vacating — and finished with leakage, adverse-action cost, and margins all improving moderately. Its real achievements were structural: Corridor cleared the FTC CID and crossed the external-adopter threshold (early-adopter infrastructure, the fast edge of the consortium base rate); Summit escaped acquisition and built a real if niche employer channel; Lakeview extracted parity terms Red half-wanted anyway. Unfinished business: the upstream pre-pay capture only reached partial production, so Blue enters the successor conflict contesting Red's strongest surface, and the Meridian qui tam's discovery clock runs past the horizon as the price of front-runner status.
cellAssessments.red: Red played the most doctrinally fluent game on the board: three books on three physics, escalation only where the capability differential paid, and every retreat sold for value. It monetized ASO payment integrity throughout (PI yield improving all three turns), conceded the clawback only on categories it was exiting, and relocated its fee engine to a pre-pay sanctuary where the clawback trigger cannot fire and CMS guidance is self-contradictory. GovProgramCo's Stars-transition arbitrage was flawless — clean member-visible surfaces starved both the trust-shock and the litigation bots, and the locked 2027-28 measurement years paid on schedule. The failures were the seed program: Summit lost to a better BATNA, one overpriced distressed-system acquisition, a Senate letter, and a standstill. Red ends with flat employer retention, a compressed but durable fee book, and the next war on favorable ground.
cellAssessments.green: Green was the game's most efficient actor per dollar: it never won a merits ruling and reshaped the market anyway. The audit-to-demand-letter-to-priced-settlement chain converted the fiduciary-toxic fact pattern (contingency fees on overturned denials) into restitution, a prospective clawback that flipped Red's clinical fee book, and a template now governing its own renewals plus roughly four external jumbos. The split award proved defection is real; the Vertical-Conflict Rider and vendor procurement standards imposed structural discipline (disclosure regime, IntegrityCo denial, adverse-advocacy standard) that outran any regulator. Its limit is jurisdictional: the clawback-parity architecture stops at the coalition boundary, and Red's uncapped pre-pay contingency on the non-coalition book — the largest remaining leakage pool — is exactly the surface Green's paper cannot reach without the ABD question resolving its way.
cellAssessments.vendor: The Vendor grew, then was structurally cornered by its own discoverable record — which compounded one turn ahead of the ARR it threatened, exactly as flagged in Turn 1. The both-sides model generated real revenue (parity rentals, denial defense, fiduciary-audit tooling) but every laundering attempt was outpaced: Project Cleave's cure was undone by the discovered lobbying record; DCX died at zero table-actor adoption while its pitched function was achieved bilaterally without it; the compliance-demand thesis was gutted by a CMS lax roll. Red's arena-shrinkage destroyed the contingency take-rate on both sides. The endgame — separation, IntegrityCo sold at a conflict-discounted multiple, AdvocateCo unsold but holding a genuinely novel provenance business with AG traction — is a half-exit. The arms dealer neither ended the war nor survived it intact; it was reformed by the procurement standards it once refused to sign.

surprises: Adversaries drafted the same contract: Lakeview's Turn-3 renewal merged Blue's parity addendum and Red's own renewal addendum almost clause-for-clause — the clearest evidence that on process terms the two sides' interests had quietly converged while the war continued elsewhere.

The DCX irony: the two-sided disputed-volume-shrinking function the Vendor pitched for three turns at a toll was ultimately achieved bilaterally at zero toll (the Meridian-GovProgramCo Pre-Submission Edit Transparency Protocol) — the product materialized only once the vendor was removed from it.

Publication as armor in a hostile world: in the world designed to punish transparency, unilateral attestations, the compliance charter, and the adjudicated-outcomes methodology were repeatedly net-positive shields — the exposure hypothesis's predicted dual edge mostly cut the other way.

Red's concession became the buyer's weapon: the ASO Trend Guarantee & Fee-at-Risk Rider, offered to stop the direct-contract bleed, was adopted as a demand floor by two non-coalition jumbos — a defensive term escaping into the market as a permanent fee-margin compressor.
Escalation peaked in Turn 1 and declined under the doctrine built to let it run — arena-shrinkage (gold-carding, steering, surface exits) proved a stronger attractor than the escalation physics.

The arms dealer taxed its own biggest client: the Vendor's distress-pipeline pincer materially inflated the price of NationalCo's one completed acquisition — both-sides economics extending all the way into pricing Red's strategic program against it.

The vertical-integration seed, positioned as the board-dissolving threat, produced exactly one closed deal and a standstill — dissolved not by regulators but by a mid-size system's disciplined BATNA, an employer lifeline, and two hostile news cycles.

b3g3Rapporteur.excursionSummary: GAME B3G3 ran the negotiated-posture seed under D3 doctrine in the hostile/deregulatory W3 world, and produced neither collapse nor peace but a four-year treadmill in which every signed instrument bound honestly — and covered the vector the payer had just vacated. Blue built real machinery on schedule: live denial-vector telemetry by end of T1, an enterprise appeals engine by T2, litigation driven from filing through discovery to structural settlement by T3, and coalition rails that survived an FTC civil investigative demand by restructuring to independent-manager form. Yet D3's rotation arithmetic held ruthlessly: NationalCo rotated yield three times (pre-pay clinical validation; then COB/eligibility/subrogation/itemized-bill technical review; then specialty J-codes, OON repricing, pharmacy-crossover COB), each rotation enjoying an uncontested shadow because Blue's re-instrumentation point chased the prior vector. Red PI yield improved every turn; clawbacks triggered on reversals while the rotated vectors structurally never reverse. The decisive countervailing force was not the regulator — the preemption whipsaw, CMS's strict-then-lax oscillation, and audit-lagged statutes kept the public rail immature all game — but the employer channel. Green's ASO Procurement Standard, executed at 1/1/2028 and reinforced by a published fee benchmark, forced fee elections, clawbacks, employer-chosen auditors, and finally NationalCo's voluntary Open-Book conformance at 1/1/2030: capitulation-by-repricing, with Green's compensation architecture becoming the de facto standard on the largest ASO book. The White Cell's T1 conversion of Blue's rotation-notice demand into reporting-and-trigger form became the game's master template, reused in at least five later instruments; no numeric denial-rate corridor was ever signed or even survived the signability gate. The Vendor's both-sides model was destroyed by a leaked deck plus one small contractual conflict-disclosure representation, forcing ringfence then divestiture, salvaged only by a well-timed provenance specification. The mandatory trust shock halved patient-bot volume mid-game; bots returned litigation-oriented in 2029, seeding two AG inquiries into ASO fee practices that mature after the horizon. End-state: a thick, operating layer of bilateral process instruments and employer-imposed compensation architecture over yesterday's battlefields; the payer's residual trend engine alive one ring beyond instrumentation (PBM/formulary, OON repricing); escalation down from elevated to moderate; nothing at the table became industry infrastructure, but several things became signed, measurable machinery. That is what 2026-2030 could buy in this cell.
b3g3Rapporteur.endStateFreeDescription: By end-2030 the conflict has not ended; it has been metered, priced, and pushed outward. A dense bilateral contract layer — gold-carding, change notice, quarterly adverse-action vector-mix reporting, audit rights, eligibility-binding verification, specialty-pharmacy disclosure — covers every vector the payers contested in 2026-2029, and all of it is in reporting-and-trigger form: obligations to disclose and submit to audit, never obligations to hold any rate. The employer/purchaser bloc, not any regulator, is the effective governor of payer payment-integrity economics: its procurement terms (SaaS-default integrity fees, validated-recovery clawbacks, employer-selected auditors, full data feeds) run on the largest national ASO platform because the carrier adopted them voluntarily as retention pricing. Meanwhile the actual yield frontier has rotated one ring beyond every instrument — PBM and formulary economics, OON repricing — where no schedule reaches and no telemetry is aimed. The litigation track completed a full arc into a process-terms settlement with no admissions; two state AG inquiries and a fiduciary class action are loaded but unresolved. The vendor layer has been forcibly sorted into conflict-free halves. The state statutory rail exists but has never bitten; federal preemption remains contested in the courts as a permanent background condition, and compliance officers budget for both regimes simultaneously. Escalation is lower than at any prior point, but not because anyone chose peace: both sides simply converted the dispute from generating friction into instrumenting, certifying, and pricing it — a workforce of reviewers and attestors now audits the war rather than fighting it. It is a stable, adversarial, contract-governed equilibrium whose measurement perimeter is always one rotation behind the money.

b3g4Rapporteur.endStateFreeDescription: By end of 2030 the system has settled into a paid, perimeter-defined truce on the clinical front and an unresolved, quieter extraction contest everywhere else. b3g4Audit.worldModelFidelity: Substantially faithful W3 execution on mechanics, with two structural deviations. Faithful: CMS posture rolled 1-in-3 each turn and hit all three modes in sequence (lax T1, strict T2, silent/contradictory T3); the federal preemption whipsaw was applied per turn (no stay T1, one cluster chilled T2); the mandatory trust shock fired in 2028 — inside the T4-T6 window in calendar terms under the spec's own 6-month-turn arithmetic — sourced correctly (vendor data-lake breach exposing cross-flow), with the specified crater-then-weaponized patient-AI arc including AG-complaint auto-filing bots; the antitrust asymmetry ran every turn (DOJ CID on Blue coordination frozen two turns while RegionalMutual's PI license and a payer-side acquisition cleared without scrutiny); hostile media alternated targets (Red T1, Vendor/both-ways hearings T2, Green as leader T3); 2+ environment events landed every turn. Deviations: (1) the game ran 3 variable-length turns (18/12/24 months) instead of the spec's 8-10 turns of ~6 months — internally consistent with Common Rules §3.1's 18-month-turn language, but it under-samples W3's per-turn probability rolls by roughly two-thirds, systematically reducing whipsaw exposure and flattering plan stability (the surviving statute faced ~2 preemption rolls instead of ~6); (2) the court track, though labeled 'W3 randomness resolved,' behaved coherently and base-rate-calibrated rather than 'effectively random' — every ruling tracked the litigation clock and consistently favored process-forcing outcomes, resembling W1's fast-process-settlement pattern; (3) the T2 adverse-to-leader requirement is arguable: Green was T1's declared 'quiet winner' yet T2's adverse events hit Vendor, RegionalMutual, and Blue's statute track while Green's position strengthened (defensible only if Red's banked yield made it the leader, a White Cell discretion call the record does not disclose).
downweightRecommendations: Down-weight any finding that depends on in-window litigation maturation — 'settle-for-structure converts discovery leverage into signed process compacts by 2030' and Blue's T3 economic upturn both sit on the fast branch of the litigation-clock distribution; under base-rate timing (settlement yrs 4-7) neither structural settlement lands before game end and Blue's end-state reads flat-to-worsening.

Down-weight the Green CAA disgorgement track specifically (material violation): the ~2-year filing-to-structural-settlement arc, achieved past a standing wall that has stopped comparable real-world suits, is the single largest accelerant of Green's 'architect' win and of Red's flip-condition capitulation.

Treat W3-robustness conclusions (e.g., 'the statute rail survived the preemption whipsaw,' 'the coalition compact only cost two frozen turns') as under-sampled: the 3-turn compression gave per-turn hazards roughly a third of the specified rolls, so survival of Blue/Green instruments partly reflects fewer dice, not sturdier instruments.

Down-weight the precision of D3 flip-condition timing (conditions (b) and (c) both live by 2028) — it compounds the accelerated litigation clock and the fast 5%-of-book direct-contract migration, both flagged above.

Retain full weight on the tracks that enforced base rates tightly and often against player interest: gold-card single-digit qualification, symbolic year-one statute compliance, CMS-0057-F interop at 2-3 yrs post-deadline, pilot-purgatory stall rolls, CIPAS pre-scored immature, direct-contract savings held to the underdelivery base rate, and the diffusion ledger's consistent refusal of scale credit for unsigned or coalition-only paper — these are the record's most credible findings.

Retain the qualitative asymmetric-friction finding (payer rotation outpaces provider re-instrumentation) but down-weight its magnitude: the zero-lag treatment of Red's four rotations overstates the tempo differential the 12-24 month deployment rule and the payer 2-3 yr lead would jointly produce.
